newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Three killed, 14 wounded in S.African Zulu march.
newsitem.headline: Three killed, 14 wounded in S.African Zulu march.

text.p: Three people were killed and 14 wounded in a Zulu nationalist march called on Wednesday to commemorate the death of more than 50 people during a 1994 protest ahead of South Africa's first all-race polls.

Imposing tribal headmen clad in animal skins presided over 12,000 Zulus packed who came from their township hostels and swarmed through Johannesburg's main streets, thrusting spears, sticks and cowhide shields into the air to the rhythm of deep chants under gloomy skies.

"We definitely confirm three deaths. Twelve people were wounded by gunshot and another two by assegais (spears). Several people were also injured by assaults," police spokesman Chris Wilken told a news conference after the march.

Violence first erupted in the sprawling Soweto township outside Johannesburg early in the morning when gunshots were fired from various workers hostels. Two people were killed and two more injured, one of them a 15-year-old boy shot in the leg.

As the trains moved through the township railway stations stray shots fired by over-ardent Zulu supporters hit and wounded eight others. At a station in Johannesburg, a person was killed by these wild bullets.

The commemoration speeches in the soul of Johannesburg city, the Library Gardens -- where several protesters were killed in the 1994 pre-election march -- were marked by anger that nobody had yet been arrested for the killings.

"We are gathered here today once more to remember with deep sorrow and sadness the brutal, cruel slaughter of men by men. We shall commemorate this day for generations to come," Prince Vanana Zulu told the crowds. "There is no reason on earth why there has been no arrest."

At least 55 people were killed as well as the hundreds injured in and around Johannesburg during the 1994 demonstration when supporters of the mainly Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party marched in support of Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini.

This time, razor wire protected the front of the headquarters of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC), where eight Zulu demonstrators were killed by security guards during the 1994 march.
President Nelson Mandela told parliament months later that he had ordered security guards to protect Shell House, headquarters of his ruling African National Congress (ANC), against any attack.
The attorney-general launched a probe into the shootings, but no one has yet been prosecuted.

"We demand that President Mandela be prosecuted for the Shell House massacre, because it was he who commanded his soldiers to kill innocent people. He must...tell the country why he ordered gunfire on the Zulu nation," Swear Manqele, a member of a Zulu "self-protection force", told Reuters.
As the last wreath was laid, the skies broke with heavy rain and resounded with bursts of wild gunshots fired into the air.

When a sustained volley of gunfire was heard for around two minutes, scores of people flung themselves to the ground for cover and heavily armed police, who had kept a vigilant presence throughout the protest, cocked their rifles.
Police and eyewitnesses confirmed that policemen on the scene had not returned fire.
The ruling party criticised the march organisers for failing to ensure the protest was peaceful, saying in a statement:

"The demonstration has left a trail of blood in and around Johannesburg. Long before the scheduled time of the march, demonstrators were spreading panic by assaulting, wounding, scores of innocent people."
Financial markets earlier said news of the killings had weakened the rand and bond markets. But the markets calmed in the afternoon as dealers digested Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's maiden budget.
